 Economy Tax agency wants to extend CBS payment deadline by 30 days
 Government plans to send Congress bill allowing payment based on estimated tax credits
 Por Beatriz Olivon , Lu Aiko Otta e Giordanna Neves — Brasília 12/11/2026 09h19 Atualizado 12/11/2026 09h19 
 Facebook 
 Twitter

 Linkedin 
 Follow on Federal Revenue Service chief Robinson Barreirinhas warns postponing collection would cost R$60bn in missed tax revenue — Foto: Valor Brazil’s Federal Revenue Service plans to send Congress a complementary bill making it easier to pay the Contribution on Goods and Services (CBS) in 2027. The idea is to let companies pay the tax based on estimated credits in the month following the transactions, leaving adjustments and final payment for the second month after, which would extend the current deadline by 30 days. If approved, the measure will be optional and allow provisional use of tax credits even before suppliers’ payment is confirmed. 
 Pending issues with tax reform are fueling business worries 
 Lawmakers rule out delay to consumption tax overhaul 
 Petrobras seeks transition period to understand tax reform 
 The postponement of fiscal document issuance for some sectors, a compliance program and the publication of the new version of the CBS regulation by the end of this week were also announced by Federal Revenue Service chief Robinson Barreirinhas at a press conference on Wednesday (11). He again denied that the reform will be postponed and addressed some points that taxpayers had complained about. 
 The complementary bill is meant to protect taxpayers with regard to the use of credits. Under the tax reform, companies will only be able to offset credits on their purchases against the tax due on their sales once it is confirmed that suppliers have actually paid the CBS. 
 To ensure that credits can be used during the transition, the Revenue Service’s main recommendation is that companies use Payment by the Acquirer (RAD), a mechanism that allows the buyer to pay the CBS on the purchase directly, rather than leaving the payment to the supplier. The amount of the tax is deducted from the payment to the supplier, guaranteeing the buyer the tax credit. According to Barreirinhas, RAD is already available to all companies and its use is optional. 
 Use of RAD is considered especially important while split payment is not fully implemented. Split payment will automatically separate and collect the tax at the moment of payment to the supplier, guaranteeing use of the credit. But the financial sector expects the mechanism to start operating on an optional basis in the second half of 2027. As it becomes available, the Revenue Service’s recommendation is that companies begin using it. 
 To prevent taxpayers from paying the tax on the full value of their sales in the meantime, without deducting the tax on the inputs they purchased, the Revenue Service will propose in the complementary bill an alternative that will allow companies to calculate the CBS taking purchase credits into account, even without confirmation that suppliers have paid. Payment will be made by estimate in the month following the transactions. 
 In the following month, the assisted assessment system will verify which taxes were actually paid and report the available credits. If a supplier has not paid the CBS, the corresponding credit will be “disallowed” and the company will have to adjust the amount due. 
 The proposal is that this alternative be available throughout 2027, with the possibility of an extension if difficulties persist in implementing split payment. The Revenue Service expects that, as that mechanism advances, the need to resort to estimated credits will diminish. 
 Barreirinhas also stressed that the Finance Ministry opposes a general postponement of the tax reform, which is being requested by some sectors of the economy, because it considers the measure unnecessary at this time. 
 A postponement would cost at least R$60 billion, according to Barreirinhas. Of that amount, R$50 billion corresponds to the reduction in the compliance gap, one of the reform’s main gains. Another R$10 billion refers to the cashback that would not be paid to low-income Brazilians in the event of a postponement. The secretary made the statements while commenting on an open letter from 74 productive-sector organizations calling for a delay. 
 Also according to Barreirinhas, dialogue with the sectors was the basis for the Revenue Service’s decision to push back to March the requirement for several fiscal documents related to the tax reform. Postponed were all Simples Nacional documents other than those for services, digital platform service invoices, municipal public transportation invoices and invoices for the transfer of real estate. 
 Between January and February, companies in these groups will continue to issue fiscal documents as they do today. “The Revenue Service’s system is ready, but we recognize that these companies’ systems may not be,” Barreirinhas said. 
 The agency will also develop a simplified model to allow companies to make adjustments to the assisted CBS assessment. The assisted assessment works like a pre-filled tax return based on companies’ fiscal documents. Currently, corrections have to be made document by document. With the simplified module, taxpayers will be able to supplement information and make adjustments to the assessment to ensure the tax is calculated correctly. 
 A compliance program and an artificial intelligence chat to answer questions are expected to support the transition to the tax reform. The compliance program is still under discussion with the IBS Management Committee for launch as a national program. But if that is not possible, a CBS-only version will be launched between this week and next. 
 The idea is not to punish taxpayers who have acted in good faith, he said. The guidance is that, when in doubt, companies should act as they always have and not withhold data from the Revenue Service. If a different interpretation of the rule is adopted later, there will be no retroactive effect to the detriment of the taxpayer. 
 According to Anderson Trautman Cardoso of Souto Correa Advogados, the announced measures show concern for the demands of the productive sector but do not fully resolve them. In his view, although a transition regime, a compliance program and the postponement of fiscal document issuance for some sectors have been proposed, difficulties remain, such as implementing by January the systems needed to meet the obligations, even if final payment of the CBS is delayed by one month. 
 “Let’s wait and see whether the business sector’s concerns are eased by the next version of the IBS and CBS regulations, which were announced for this week,” he said. 
 Marcos Maia , a partner at law firm Maneira Advogados, notes that this is not a general postponement of the reform, nor necessarily a tax advantage granted to specific economic sectors. “The three situations each have their own reasons for additional time,” he said. On the Simples Nacional regime, for example, he says that in retail, goods invoices already exist, but systems need to be adjusted to the new information. 
 For Douglas Mota , a partner at law firm Demarest, the announced measures help taxpayers plan the transition better. “While there is clearly a feeling among taxpayers that postponing would be best, the difficulty of a situation like this is also understood. So by announcing that there will be no fines for good-faith errors made during the transition, the Revenue Service offers at least some relief.”
